> 和大怨，必有餘怨；安可以為善？

Chapter 78 was water taking the mud and clearing. Chapter 79 is about the thing that keeps the account: a piece of wood.

## 契 is a tally split in two

契: 大約也 — a binding. 約 is to wrap, to tie two things together.

And 契's old form is built on 㓞 — to cut. A piece of wood is notched, split down the middle, and each party keeps one half. Bring the halves together and the notches match.

So a 契 is inherently a half. It cannot be used alone. All of its value is in the other piece.

The word appears in the book only here, and it is the only word in the book for a written claim.

## 聖人執左契，而不責於人

The sage holds the left half and does not demand from the person.

責 is to press for payment — the character carries the sense of a demand that has an edge on it.

The sentence is the quietest act of self-restraint in the whole book. It is not magnanimity; it is not generosity. It is: he is fully entitled to ask, and does not ask.

Which is a very different thing from being unable to ask, and the difference is the entire chapter.

## 有德司契，無德司徹

With 德, one keeps the tally; without 德, one keeps the 徹.

徹 is to go through, to take everything — the tax that goes through the fields and leaves nothing behind.

So the contrast is not between forgiving and unforgiving. It is between holding a record and emptying the account.

## 和大怨，必有餘怨

Reconcile a great grievance, and there will be residual grievance.

To make peace after the harm is done leaves the remainder, because the harm itself is still in the record.

安可以為善 — how can that be called good?

The chapter's answer is upstream: the good is done where the grievance was never created. Which is chapter 64's 治之於未亂, applied to relations.

## 天道無親，常與善人

The way of heaven has no favorites; it is constantly with the good person.

無親 is not indifference. 親, as in chapter 56's 不可得而親, is the relation established by proximity and preference. Heaven has no such relation to anyone.

與 is to be with, to accompany — and also, as in chapter 68, a pairing of hands.

So the line is not a reward system. It is: the one whose way has no favorites is the one who can be accompanied.

## Why this follows 78

78: receive the mud and let it settle; nothing can be substituted for it.
79: and do not keep the tally against the person who gave it.

Both are the same refusal to hold an account. One refuses the account of grievance; the other refuses the account of debt.

## A test

Take a grievance you consider settled. Ask whether you still hold the other half of the wood — the memory with the notch cut in it, kept somewhere. The chapter's instrument is simple: if the half is still in the drawer, the reconciliation is not done.
